quote: Don't reach for an antipsychotic before excluding hypoglycemia, hypoxia, delirium, withdrawal, pain, and akathisia.
problem: The one thing on this list that must be excluded before a D2 blocker is given — catatonia — is the only thing missing. Excited catatonia presents exactly as this page's scenario (agitation with normal vitals and no delirium), and an antipsychotic given to a catatonic patient can precipitate malignant catatonia/NMS. The identical omission runs through the ruleOut card (Hypoglycemia / Hypoxia / Delirium / Intoxication-withdrawal / Pain-retention / Akathisia). The site's own resident PRN trainer contradicts this page: it makes catatonia a named etiology, hard-flags D2 blockers in it, and calls missing it "a stereotyped, high-harm error."
replacement: Don't reach for an antipsychotic before excluding hypoglycemia, hypoxia, delirium, withdrawal, pain, akathisia, and catatonia — excited catatonia looks like agitation, and a D2 blocker can tip it into malignant catatonia/NMS.
basis: Heckers S, Walther S. Catatonia. N Engl J Med. 2023 (antipsychotics precipitate/worsen catatonia; benzodiazepine, not D2 blockade, is the first move). Project BETA psychopharmacology consensus (Wilson 2012): agent choice follows etiology. Internal inconsistency with this library's own rp-agitation trainer, which lists catatonia in its etiology bank and sets a hazardIf on D2 blockers for it.

quote: "older_dementia": "All antipsychotics carry FDA black-box mortality warning in dementia-related psychosis."
problem: The second-generation antipsychotic choice carries no hazard or caution for parkinson_dlb or for catatonia — only a QTc caution and the dementia black-box. In the Parkinson scenario (populationFlags parkinson_dlb + older_dementia) a resident who picks "Second-generation antipsychotic" is told nothing about parkinsonism worsening or neuroleptic sensitivity; the pack flags only typical antipsychotics as hazardous there, which reads as a licence for risperidone or olanzapine — the two SGAs most likely to cause a severe, sometimes fatal, neuroleptic sensitivity reaction in DLB/PD. In the catatonia scenario the same choice draws no flag at all, even though the scenario's own teaching point says to recognise catatonia before reaching for an antipsychotic. This is the failure mode a hazard-avoidance trainer exists to prevent. Note the two added keys belong in a hazardIf block on this choice (as they are for d2_typical), not cautionIf, so pharmVerdict returns hard=true.
replacement:
"older_dementia": "All antipsychotics carry FDA black-box mortality warning in dementia-related psychosis.",
     "parkinson_dlb": "Not a safe default here — risperidone, olanzapine and higher-dose quetiapine all block D2 and can trigger severe neuroleptic sensitivity in Parkinson disease/Lewy body dementia. If an antipsychotic is unavoidable the choice is narrow (quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin) and belongs to your attending.",
     "catatonia": "Second-generation agents also precipitate/worsen catatonia and NMS — hold antipsychotics until catatonia is excluded or treated."
basis: Neuroleptic sensitivity reaction in DLB/PD (McKeith DLB consortium criteria; PD psychosis management favours quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin). Heckers S, Walther S. Catatonia. N Engl J Med. 2023. The pack's own d2_typical entry already encodes both hazards, so the sga entry is internally inconsistent with it.

quote: | **Management** | Stop agent · benzodiazepines · **cyproheptadine** 12 mg PO then 2 mg q2h (max ~32 mg/24h) · cooling | Stop antipsychotic · supportive cooling · benzodiazepines · **dantrolene / bromocriptine / amantadine** for severe |
problem: Three life-saving steps are absent from the row a resident will actually read at 2 a.m. (1) Serotonin syndrome: the intervention that saves the hyperthermic patient is sedation, intubation and non-depolarising neuromuscular blockade once temperature exceeds ~41.1 degrees C — heat generation is muscular, so antipyretics and cooling blankets alone fail, and succinylcholine is the wrong paralytic (rhabdomyolysis/hyperkalaemia). As written, a resident escalating temperature at 41.5 keeps giving benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine. (2) NMS: aggressive IV isotonic fluid resuscitation with CK and renal monitoring is the mainstay against rhabdomyolysis-driven AKI — the page names CK >1,000 in the labs row but never says to hydrate. (3) The trigger row correctly names abrupt dopaminergic withdrawal as an NMS cause, but management never says to restart the dopaminergic agent, which is the specific treatment for parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome.
replacement: | **Management** | Stop agent · benzodiazepines · **cyproheptadine** 12 mg PO then 2 mg q2h (max ~32 mg/24h) · cooling · **temp >41.1 °C is an airway emergency: sedate, intubate, and paralyze with a non-depolarizing agent (NOT succinylcholine — rhabdomyolysis/hyperkalemia risk); antipyretics do not work because the heat is muscular** | Stop antipsychotic — and **restart the dopaminergic agent if NMS followed its abrupt withdrawal** · **aggressive IV isotonic fluids** with serial CK/renal function for rhabdomyolysis and AKI · supportive cooling · benzodiazepines · **dantrolene / bromocriptine / amantadine** for severe · ECT for refractory |
basis: Boyer EW, Shannon M. The serotonin syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2005 (paralysis and intubation for hyperthermia >41.1 C; antipyretics ineffective; avoid physical restraints). Standard NMS management (volume resuscitation for rhabdomyolysis; dopamine agonist reinstatement in withdrawal-precipitated NMS/parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia; ECT for refractory cases).

problem: The antipsychotic-plus-benzodiazepine combination is hazard-flagged only for delirium. Its antipsychotic half carries every hazard that d2_typical carries, so a resident choosing the combination in the catatonia scenario or the Parkinson scenario is warned about nothing. The combination is also the pack's own "often most effective" option, which makes it the likely pick under pressure — the two scenarios where it is most dangerous are exactly the two where the tool stays silent.
replacement:
"delirium": "Benzodiazepine component worsens non-withdrawal delirium.",
     "catatonia": "The antipsychotic component can precipitate or worsen catatonia and NMS — give the benzodiazepine alone and hold the antipsychotic.",
     "parkinson_dlb": "The antipsychotic component carries the same D2 hazard in Parkinson disease/Lewy body dementia as a typical agent — do not use this combination here."
basis: Heckers S, Walther S. Catatonia. N Engl J Med. 2023; neuroleptic sensitivity in DLB/PD. Consistency with the pack's own d2_typical hazardIf entries.

quote: a second-generation antipsychotic is generally preferred over haloperidol for faster onset and fewer EPS
problem: The stated rationale is wrong twice over. Onset is not the SGA advantage — parenteral haloperidol acts at least as fast, and the oral SGAs a resident would actually offer are slower; the only defensible argument is the EPS burden. And the framing skips the point that changes management most: antipsychotics do not shorten delirium, reduce ICU/hospital days, or lower mortality, so the decision is whether to medicate at all, not which agent is quicker. Stated as a preference rule it invites reflexive antipsychotic dosing in an 80s post-op patient whose actual treatment is finding the cause and stopping the opioid/anticholinergic already on the list.
replacement: haloperidol and second-generation agents are both used; the case for an SGA is a lower EPS burden, not faster onset — and because no antipsychotic shortens delirium or lowers mortality, reserve one for agitation that endangers the patient or staff after non-pharmacologic measures fail, at the lowest dose for the shortest time
basis: NICE CG103 delirium (short-term haloperidol or olanzapine only when distressed and non-pharmacologic measures have failed) — a guideline this library already cites on the agitation page as nice-delirium-cg103; Agar 2017 JAMA Intern Med and the 2019 AHRQ/Nikooie systematic review (no benefit on delirium duration, cognition, or mortality).

quote: Parkinson disease on dopaminergic therapy; recent evening confusion/hallucinations.
problem: This scenario is keyed trueEtiology primary_psych, but the history given is new evening confusion in a 70s patient on dopaminergic therapy — the textbook presentation of delirium or dopaminergic drug toxicity, not of a primary psychiatric illness. A resident who correctly picks delirium is told they missed the discriminating features, in a trainer whose whole thesis is that etiology comes first. Separately, "Primary psychiatric (psychosis / mania)" is the wrong category even for clean PD/DLB psychosis, which is a secondary/neurodegenerative psychosis; if the scenario is kept, either add a distinct etiology option or key it to undetermined.
replacement: Parkinson disease on dopaminergic therapy; long-standing, non-fluctuating visual hallucinations attributed to PD psychosis. No new medication change, infection, or metabolic derangement; attention intact on exam.
basis: New fluctuating confusion in an older hospitalized adult is delirium until proven otherwise (the pack's own delirium discriminators say exactly this); PD/DLB psychosis is classified as a psychosis secondary to a neurodegenerative disorder, not a primary psychiatric illness.

quote: - **Hemodialysis** if level **>4.0** mEq/L (any patient), or **>2.5** with severe neuro/renal signs or life-threatening features.
problem: The lithium section gives thresholds and dialysis criteria but never states the management that precedes them and applies to every case: hold lithium, stop the contributing agents it just listed, and give IV isotonic saline to restore volume and renal lithium clearance. A resident using this as their bedside reference gets a decision rule about dialysis and nothing to do in the hours before nephrology answers — which is when most of the clearance is won or lost.
replacement:
- **Before dialysis is even the question:** hold lithium, stop the contributors (NSAID, thiazide, ACEi/ARB), send a level with renal function and electrolytes, and start **IV isotonic saline** to restore volume and renal lithium clearance. Repeat the level every 2–4 h until it is falling; nephrogenic diabetes insipidus can drive hypernatremia, so follow sodium as you hydrate.
- **Hemodialysis** if level **>4.0** mEq/L (any patient), or **>2.5** with severe neuro/renal signs or life-threatening features.
basis: EXTRIP workgroup recommendations on extracorporeal treatment for lithium poisoning (Decker et al., CJASN 2015) — volume repletion with isotonic saline and cessation of lithium and contributing nephrotoxins/diuretics is the baseline therapy in every case; dialysis criteria sit on top of it.

quote: - Replete **K⁺ >4.0** and **Mg²⁺ >2.0**; reconcile every QT-prolonging drug and interaction.
problem: The section is titled "QTc / torsades de pointes" but contains no treatment for torsades — the one number a resident needs at the bedside (IV magnesium sulfate 2 g, given regardless of the serum magnesium) is absent, as are overdrive pacing/isoproterenol for pause-dependent torsades and defibrillation for the unstable patient. The bullet also omits units: with lithium quoted in mEq/L eight lines above, "Mg²⁺ >2.0" invites repletion to 2.0 mEq/L (about 4.8 mg/dL) rather than the intended 2.0 mg/dL.
replacement:
- Replete **K⁺ >4.0 mEq/L** and **Mg²⁺ >2.0 mg/dL**; reconcile every QT-prolonging drug and interaction.
- **If torsades actually fires:** call the code, give **IV magnesium sulfate 2 g** over 1–2 min *regardless of the serum magnesium level*, stop every offending drug, correct K⁺ and Ca²⁺, treat pause/bradycardia dependence with overdrive pacing or isoproterenol, and defibrillate if it degenerates to sustained VT/VF.
basis: Tisdale et al., Drug-Induced Arrhythmias: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association, Circulation 2020 — the source this page already cites; ACLS polymorphic VT/torsades algorithm.

problem: Two problems in one card. First, the differential a resident is handed for the febrile, rigid, altered patient contains only drug syndromes — CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis) and heat stroke are absent, and anchoring on NMS in a febrile patient on an antipsychotic without excluding meningitis delays antibiotics in the one item on the list that kills within hours. Second, anticholinergic toxicity is forced into the differential but taught nowhere in the page body: there is no discriminator, no antidote, nothing — yet the single feature that separates it from serotonin syndrome (dry skin and absent bowel sounds versus diaphoresis and hyperactive bowel) is the highest-yield finding on this whole page.
replacement:
- Anticholinergic toxicity (dry skin, flushing, urinary retention, **absent** bowel sounds — the mirror image of serotonin syndrome's diaphoresis and hyperactive bowel)
- CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis) and heat stroke — fever + rigidity + altered mentation is not NMS until these are excluded
basis: Standard toxidrome differentiation (Boyer & Shannon NEJM 2005 for the serotonin syndrome/anticholinergic contrast); NMS is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring CNS infection to be ruled out before it is settled on.

quote: - Effective in ~90%; titrate to a standing regimen, often up to ~16 mg/day (higher only under close monitoring).
problem: Benzodiazepine response in catatonia is usually reported at roughly 60–80%, not ~90%. On a numbers page for residents the inflated figure has a direction: a resident who believes nine in ten respond will read a partial or absent response as under-dosing and keep titrating rather than moving to ECT, which is where the delay in malignant catatonia costs the patient. The page's neighbouring figure for ECT (60–100%) is oddly low-bounded for the same reason — ECT response is generally quoted at 80–100%, so as written the two numbers make benzodiazepines look better than ECT.
replacement: - Response is generally reported at roughly 60–80% — good, but not near-universal; titrate to a standing regimen, often up to ~16 mg/day (higher only under close monitoring), and treat a partial or absent response as the trigger to move to ECT rather than as a reason to keep climbing.
basis: Bush et al. 1996 catatonia treatment series and subsequent reviews report benzodiazepine response in roughly two-thirds to four-fifths of cases; ECT response is generally quoted at 80–100%. Settled by checking the response range stated in Heckers S, Walther S, Catatonia, N Engl J Med 2023 — the citation this section already rests on — and matching both figures to it.

quote: - Common contributors to incapacity: **cognitive disorders ~54%, substance use ~37%, psychosis ~25%** — many reversible (delirium, psychosis, depression). Treat the reversible cause and **reassess.**
problem: Three precise percentages are presented as epidemiology with no study, cohort, or setting attached — not even a design. A resident cannot get from these numbers to a paper, and will quote them on rounds as fact; they also sum to well over 100% with no statement that the categories overlap, and no denominator (medical inpatients? consult referrals? capacity evaluations?), which is what determines whether they mean anything at all.
replacement: - Common contributors to incapacity, in rough order of frequency: cognitive disorders (dementia, delirium), then substance intoxication/withdrawal, then psychosis and severe depression — categories that overlap in the same patient, and many of them reversible. Treat the reversible cause and **reassess.**
basis: Reviewer instruction on untraceable statistics. If the percentages are kept they need a named cohort with its denominator and setting stated (e.g. Sessums et al., JAMA 2011, gives ~26% incapacity prevalence among medical inpatients — but not this contributor breakdown).

quote: One evidence-based lever for the *next* admission is the **psychiatric advance directive (PAD)**: in a multicenter RCT, peer-worker–facilitated PADs cut compulsory admissions from **39.9% to 27.0%** over 12 months (risk difference −0.13) — worth raising with patients who have a history of involuntary holds.
problem: A specific effect size is attached to a study design ("a multicenter RCT") rather than to a study identity, so a resident who wants to check it, cite it, or judge whether it transfers to a US unit has no way to reach the paper. It also matters here because generalisability is the whole question: the trial population, the peer-worker infrastructure, and the compulsory-admission law are all context the number depends on. The same unattributed figure is repeated in the High-yield pearls list and should be fixed there too.
replacement: One evidence-based lever for the *next* admission is the **psychiatric advance directive (PAD)**: in a French multicenter RCT of adults with schizophrenia, bipolar, or schizoaffective disorder who had a compulsory admission in the prior 12 months (Tinland et al., *JAMA Psychiatry* 2022), peer-worker–facilitated PADs cut compulsory admission over 12 months from **39.9% to 27.0%** (risk difference −0.13) — worth raising with patients who have a history of involuntary holds, with the caveat that the peer-worker facilitation, not the document alone, was the intervention.
basis: Reviewer instruction: an effect size attached to a design rather than an identity is a finding. The figures match Tinland A, et al., Effect of Psychiatric Advance Statements Combined With Peer Worker Facilitation on Compulsory Admissions, JAMA Psychiatry 2022 — confirm the citation and the risk-difference sign against the paper before publishing it.

quote: - Document the reasoning behind risk and observation level, not just a score — most patients who die by suicide screen low-risk at last contact.
problem: The conclusion is right but the supporting claim overstates what the literature shows, and it is asserted with no source anywhere on the page. The defensible statements are that roughly half of suicide deaths occur among patients last categorised as low risk, and that a large share deny ideation at their final contact — two different findings from two different literatures, compressed here into one "most" that a resident will repeat in a mortality review or a deposition. Restated more precisely it is a stronger argument, not a weaker one, because the point is the poor predictive value of categorisation, not a headcount. The same sentence recurs in the page prose and again in High-yield pearls.
replacement: - Document the reasoning behind risk and observation level, not just a score — risk categorisation has poor predictive value, and about half of suicide deaths occur in patients last classified low-risk.
basis: Large et al. meta-analyses of suicide risk categorisation (roughly half of suicides occur in low-risk strata; PPV of high-risk categorisation is low); Louzon et al., Psychiatr Serv 2016, for denial of ideation at last contact. Would be settled by naming whichever of these the author intended and matching the wording to it.

quote: - **Liver disease:** prefer benzodiazepines cleared by conjugation — **"LOT": Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam** (no oxidative metabolism). **Duloxetine is contraindicated in chronic liver disease.**
problem: The liver bullet names one antidepressant to avoid and omits the psychotropic that most often causes the problem: valproate, which carries a label contraindication in significant hepatic impairment and which a consult resident is far more likely to be asked to continue in a patient with cirrhosis. It is also the drug behind hyperammonaemic encephalopathy — a picture that reads as worsening delirium and gets missed because nobody sends an ammonia level. Carbamazepine belongs in the same sentence.
replacement: - **Liver disease:** prefer benzodiazepines cleared by conjugation — **"LOT": Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam** (no oxidative metabolism), and remember even these accumulate and can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy. **Duloxetine is contraindicated in chronic liver disease.** **Valproate is contraindicated in significant hepatic impairment** — and valproate-induced hyperammonaemic encephalopathy mimics worsening delirium, so send an ammonia level, not just LFTs. Carbamazepine is a poor choice for the same reason.
basis: Valproate US label contraindication in hepatic disease/significant hepatic dysfunction; valproate-induced hyperammonaemic encephalopathy is well described and occurs with normal transaminases and therapeutic valproate levels.

quote: - Higher-risk psychotropics: **IV haloperidol, ziprasidone, thioridazine (avoid), pimozide**; **citalopram capped at 20 mg** if age >60, hepatic impairment, or CYP2C19 poor metabolizer.
problem: The list is accurate but omits the QT-prolonging drug a psychiatry resident on consults actually meets most often: methadone, whose effect is dose-dependent and which is the usual reason a patient already sits near the action threshold before anyone adds an antipsychotic. Droperidol is likewise missing. A resident who checks this reference before starting an antipsychotic in a patient on methadone maintenance sees nothing prompting a baseline ECG.
replacement: - Higher-risk psychotropics: **IV haloperidol, droperidol, ziprasidone, thioridazine (avoid), pimozide** — and the one a psychiatry resident meets most often, **methadone** (dose-dependent; it is usually why the QTc is already long before you add anything, so get a baseline ECG before layering an antipsychotic on top); **citalopram capped at 20 mg** if age >60, hepatic impairment, or CYP2C19 poor metabolizer.
basis: Tisdale et al., Circulation 2020 (the AHA statement this section cites) lists methadone and droperidol among the agents with known torsades risk; methadone QT monitoring is a standard element of OUD treatment guidance.

quote: Match the patient to the least restrictive level of care that is safe: inpatient → partial hospitalization (PHP) / intensive outpatient (IOP) → residential → assertive community treatment (ACT) or community case management → supportive housing or group home → routine outpatient.
problem: Written with arrows this reads as a descending restrictiveness gradient, and it is mis-ordered: residential treatment is a 24-hour supervised setting and is *more* restrictive than PHP or IOP, which the patient goes home from at night. It also mixes two different axes — treatment intensity (inpatient, residential, PHP, IOP, outpatient) with wraparound services (ACT, case management, supportive housing) that attach at several intensities rather than sitting between them. A resident using this as the least-restrictive-alternative ladder can step someone "down" from PHP into residential and document it as the less restrictive option.
replacement: Match the patient to the least restrictive level of care that is safe — and note you are choosing two things, not one. Treatment intensity descends inpatient → residential → partial hospitalization (PHP) → intensive outpatient (IOP) → routine outpatient (residential is *more* restrictive than PHP/IOP, not less). Wraparound supports layer onto any of those: assertive community treatment (ACT) or community case management, supportive housing or a group home, peer support.
basis: ASAM/LOCUS-style level-of-care continua and ordinary US behavioural-health practice: residential is a 24-hour supervised level of care above partial hospitalization; ACT is a service model delivered in the community, not a step on the restrictiveness ladder.

quote: Note that HIPAA permits sharing for treatment, payment, and operations.
problem: On a confidentiality page for residents on an adult inpatient unit, HIPAA's treatment/payment/operations permission is stated without the exception that actually catches people: records from a federally assisted substance use disorder treatment program fall under 42 CFR Part 2, which is stricter than HIPAA and governs a large share of the co-occurring patients on the unit. A resident who takes "treatment, payment, and operations" as the whole rule will repeat SUD treatment information to an outside provider or a family member without the consent Part 2 requires — the most common confidentiality error made by trainees on an inpatient unit, and one with regulatory consequences the page never signals.
replacement: Note that HIPAA permits sharing for treatment, payment, and operations — but two carve-outs matter on an inpatient unit: **42 CFR Part 2** governs records originating from a federally assisted substance use disorder treatment program and has its own consent requirements (recent rulemaking aligns it more closely with HIPAA, so verify the current rule and whether your program is a Part 2 program), and psychotherapy notes are separately protected. Assume SUD-treatment information needs its own consent before you repeat it.
basis: 42 CFR Part 2 confidentiality of substance use disorder patient records; the 2024 Part 2 final rule aligns consent for treatment/payment/operations more closely with HIPAA — confirm the current rule text and local applicability, which is what would settle the exact wording here.
